asDecan.p: Your Sun sits between 20 and 29 degrees of Virgo, the closing third of the sign. Each sign is split into three ten-degree decans, each with a planet and a numbered card, and in the Chaldean order this last one goes to Mercury. Mercury already rules Virgo and is exalted there too, which is unusual. A planet in its own sign and its exaltation at once works at full strength with nothing in its way, so these degrees are about as Mercurial as the zodiac gets. Virgo being earth, the thinking goes into things you can hold, the filing cabinet, the will, the family recipe written out properly. The Eight of Pentacles opens the sign learning a craft, and the Nine is off enjoying the garden it paid for. Yours closes Virgo leaning toward Libra and other people. Look at the card, three generations under one archway, and you can see why this slice keeps asking who the careful work is for. The Hermit is still your Sun card underneath.

You're the one who knows where the documents are. When a parent goes into hospital, it's you who has the Medicare card, the list of tablets and the name of the GP within about ten minutes. At a family dinner you're quietly keeping track of whose birthday is next and whether anyone has actually booked the restaurant for it. There's a shared spreadsheet somewhere with your name on it, for the holiday house or the footy club or the renovation, and you update it when nobody asks. On a free weekend you might scan a shoebox of old photos and label every one with names and years, because in twenty years nobody will remember who that is standing next to Nan. That's Mercury at full strength in an earth sign. You notice the gap, the insurance that lapsed last year, the form nobody signed, and it nags at you until it's fixed.

Everyone knows you're organised. Fewer people notice how well you talk across the generations of a family. Mercury is the go-between planet, and in these degrees you can explain your grandmother to your teenage niece and the other way round, so both of them come away a bit softer. You're often the one who gets the old stories written down, asks your uncle about the farm before it's too late, and finds out why two branches of the family stopped speaking in 1987. You can sit an eighty-year-old and a sixteen-year-old down with the photo albums and keep both of them interested for an hour. At a funeral it's usually you who gets the dates right in the eulogy and still finds the story that makes the room laugh, and afterwards three cousins ask you for a copy.

Sometimes you end up running a family, or a team, as if it were an estate you'd been left in charge of. You make decisions for everyone because you've got the information and they don't, and it slowly stops occurring to you to ask. Your siblings find out Mum's aged care has been sorted when you tell them it's done. Your partner learns the super has moved to a different fund after the forms have gone in. You meant it as care, and a lot of the time it is. But people start to feel managed, and some of them stop bringing you their own ideas. It costs you too. Ask yourself what you'd like for your own birthday and there's a long pause, because you've spent the year sorting out everyone else's.

When something goes badly wrong, a death in the family, a business folding, a divorce with a house in the middle of it, you go to the paperwork first. You find the will, ring the bank, get certified copies, make the folder. For a week that's a real service and everyone leans on you. The trouble comes about ten days in, when the admin is under control and the grief hasn't been touched at all. You start checking the folder again, re-reading the same emails, snapping at your brother because he's lost the form you sent him twice. The people around you feel shut out, because you've turned a loss into a project and there's no job for them in it. What helps is someone sitting with you with the papers put away, and a meal cooked by somebody else. If it's a death, talking about the actual person, their bad jokes, the way they drove, usually lets the crying start.

With Libra only a few degrees off, you're more partnership-minded than the earlier slices of Virgo, and you think about love as a shared life that works day to day. What partners don't expect is how far ahead you've thought. By the third date you might already be wondering, privately, whether their family would get on with yours at Christmas. It isn't coldness. It's Mercury doing what it does, making plans, and once you care about someone they're in the plans. You show love by folding a person into your arrangements, a key cut for them, their name on the calendar on the fridge, their mum's birthday remembered without a reminder. What you find harder is love that's untidy, like the partner who wants to drive off somewhere on a Saturday with no plan. Go along with it now and then, and notice that you usually enjoy it by the second day.

The work that fits these degrees has a long tail and a lot of detail. Estate law, archives, family businesses, superannuation, genealogy, running a practice that's been in the same town for forty years. Mercury is the planet of contracts and records, and at full strength in Virgo it likes the kind that will still matter in fifty years. You're the one who writes the handover document everyone else skips, and six months after you've moved on, people are still using it. You also tend to ask the question nobody else in the meeting wants to, which is what happens to all of this when the founder retires. What goes wrong is that you become the only person who understands how things work, and then you can't take leave without the place wobbling. Train your replacement early, before there's even a title for the job, and write down the bits only you know.

In your twenties these degrees can feel old for their age. You had a proper filing system at twenty-two and were worrying about super before your friends had a savings account, and people teased you for it. By the mid-thirties that usually pays off, and it often comes with responsibility arriving early, a parent to help, a family property, a business someone wants you to take over. That's also the stage where plenty of people with this decan discover they've been building somebody else's idea of a legacy. The fifties tend to bring a sorting. You look at what you've been keeping for everyone, the house, the traditions, the boxes in the garage, and decide what you'd actually like to hand on. A lot of late Virgo Suns get lighter and funnier around then, and closer to the youngest people in the family.

Pick one object you'd like someone to have after you, a ring, a cast iron pan, a book with your notes in the margins. Write a short card to go with it, a few lines on where it came from and why it matters to you, and tape it underneath or tuck it inside. Then tell the person, out loud, that it's theirs one day. Do just the one, however tempting it is to start a list. Notice afterwards how long you spent on those few lines.
